paper_title: Your Policy Is Secretly a Harness: The Decision Geometry of Agent Interfaces

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Language model agents are post-trained and deployed through a harness, the prompts, tools, and control logic that present a task to the model and execute its outputs. Harnesses are often revised and judged by how an already trained model performs under them, which assumes that what the model learned under one harness carries over to the next. We ask what a policy learns from its harness and what survives when the harness changes. Under KL-regularized control, we show that the log odds of an optimal policy recover how strongly its harness favors each action over the others, so a trained policy carries the preferences of its harness. Deployed return then equals the ceiling of the harness, the best return it offers, minus the mismatch of the policy, the return lost to its own suboptimal decisions. Training changes only the mismatch, while changing the harness moves both terms. Comparing harnesses with a fixed model therefore mixes what each harness offers with how well that model uses it. In MiniWoB++, post-training makes a model's preferences specific to its training harness. Reversing the order of the observation fields leaves every optimal decision unchanged yet lowers a trained model's success from 85.0% to 19.2%. Conversely, every new harness that a fixed-model comparison rejects but that raises the ceiling outperforms the original agent after further training under it, and ceiling and mismatch measured beforehand predict these gains. For coding-agent harnesses on Terminal-Bench Lite, ceiling minus mismatch estimated with a stronger model as a stand-in for the optimum reproduces the accuracy ranking, while either term alone does not. Code is available at https://github.com/2020-qqtcg/HRP.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Language model agents are post-trained and deployed through harness, the prompts, tools, and control logic that present task to the model and execute its outputs. Interface design and prompt formatting change agent performance (Yang et al., 2024; Sclar et al., 2024). Automated harness design revises prompts, tools, and workflows and scores each candidate by how fixed model performs under it (Hu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025b; Fernando et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2026). Such score assumes that what the model learned under earlier harnesses carries over to each candidate, yet the same interface change can raise one models accuracy and lower that of fine-tuned model (Mu et al., 2025). At the same time, training can move behavior that prompt or harness supplies into the weights (Snell et al., 2022; Ye et al., 2026), and recent methods adapt harnesses and weights together (Hebbar et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026; Kim et al., 2026). These practices raise the question we study: What does policy learn from its harness, and what survives when the harness changes? Two experiments make the question concrete. In the first, we take web agent post-trained under one harness and reverse the order of the fields in its observation, JSON object with fields such as the Corresponding author: yaoshu@hkust-gz.edu.cn. 1 task instruction, the page state, and the available actions. The fields keep their contents. We also hold fixed the actions, their execution, the rewards, and the reference policy that regularizes training, so every optimal decision stays the same. The model still changes its most probable action at about half of the states, and its task success falls from 85.0% to 19.2%. Keeping the decisions model should make does not keep the decisions it makes. In the second, new harness adds batched clicks, which execute two clicks in one decision. The new actions raise the best achievable return, yet the trained models success drops when we move it to the new harness without changing its weights. frozen comparison, which evaluates candidate harnesses with the same trained weights, would therefore reject the new harness. We then train the model further for the same budget under each harness, starting from the same trained weights, which we call the source checkpoint. We call further training under the new harness adaptation, and further training under the original harness continuation. The adapted model succeeds more often than both the source checkpoint and the continued one. The harness that first hurt the model gives the best agent. Figure 1 shows the task success at each step, with the new harness as Harness 1. Figure 1: Adaptation reverses frozen comparison. The left group evaluates the model trained under Harness 0, the source checkpoint, under both harnesses with its weights frozen. The right group evaluates the models after equal further training under each harness. The dotted line marks the source checkpoints success under Harness 0, and colors mark the evaluation harness. We explain both results in the control problem that harness induces over semantic actions, the operations an agent executes together with their arguments. Under KL-regularized control, the optimal policy is softmax over action scores. Each score adds an actions long-term value to its log probability under the reference policy, so an optimal policys log odds between two actions are proportional to the difference of their scores. policy trained to optimality under harness therefore carries the relative action scores that the harness induces, even though it contains none of the harnesss code, tools, or execution machinery. In this sense, policy is secretly harness. In our controlled study, real post-training moves models action scores toward the optimum of its training harness, and each harness leaves its own preferences in the model. Action scores also show why trained policy can fail after it is moved to new harness. The scores policy carries are the ones it expresses through its training interface, which we call its readout through that interface, and the same weights can express different scores through another interface. policy is thus secretly its training harness, as read through that harness. new harness can therefore change which actions are optimal, by moving the optimal scores, and separately change which actions the model picks, by moving the readout. Reversing the observation fields leaves the optimal scores in place and moves only the readout. Scores fix decisions but not how much return harness offers, since raising every reward by the same constant changes no decision. To convert score changes into return, we therefore add this value back by applying the regularized performance-gap identity (Geist et al., 2019; ODonoghue, 2022) to the harness-induced problem. Deployed return equals the harnesss ceiling C, the best return any policy can reach under it, minus the policys mismatch , the return the policy loses by departing from the optimal policy. The mismatch is the KL divergence Figure 2: harness revision and weight update act on different terms. Summit heights are the ceilings, the robots altitude is its return, and the gap between them is the mismatch. Moving the trained model to the new harness with frozen weights (① to ②) raises the ceiling but lowers the return. Updating the weights under the new harness (② to ③) lowers only the mismatch. The adapted model beats the source checkpoint under the original harness once its mismatch falls below , the new ceiling minus the source checkpoints return under the original harness. from the optimal policy, accumulated along the policys own trajectories. The ceiling does not depend on the models weights, so training under fixed harness changes only , while harness change can move both terms. frozen comparison of harnesses therefore mixes what each harness offers with how well the current checkpoint uses it. In the batched-click example, the new harness raises the ceiling slightly but raises the frozen models mismatch about ten times as much, so return falls. Adaptation then lowers the mismatch, and once the mismatch falls below threshold we derive, the adapted model beats the original model under the original harness. Figure 2 illustrates both steps. Our contributions are as follows. 1. What policy learns under harness. The log odds of an optimal policy identify exactly the relative action scores that harness induces. These scores fix every decision but not how much return the harness offers, which Contribution 3 adds back as the ceiling. On MiniWoB++, post-training moves the models action preferences toward the training harnesss optimum and makes them specific to that harness. 2. Why transfer fails. We split the score error of policy moved to new harness into three parts. The target shift is the change in the optimal scores, the training residual is the error that training under the original harness left behind, and the readout drift is the change in the scores that the model expresses. Presentation changes that keep every optimal decision isolate the readout drift, and they alone can make trained model fail on most tasks. 3. What transfer costs and how to measure it. Deployed return equals ceiling minus mismatch exactly. From this identity we derive the mismatch threshold below which adaptation turns harness revision that hurt the frozen model into gain. Adaptation to batched clicks crosses this threshold and outperforms continued training under the original harness. We also move trained checkpoints between six harnesses. Among the moves that frozen comparison rejects, ceiling and mismatch measured before adaptation predict which ones adaptation makes beneficial. Mismatch estimated from sampled actions predicts return changes when the optimum is known. For coding agents, where no optimum is available, estimates that put stronger teacher model in the optimums place order five harnesses by Terminal-Bench Lite accuracy.

sections.title: 7 DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION
sections.content: A policy trained under harness learns the harnesss relative action scores and expresses them through its interface. Post-training makes these preferences harness-specific, and new interface can change the models choices even when every optimal decision stays the same. Because deployed return is the ceiling minus the mismatch, harness that offers more can hurt trained model and become the best choice after adaptation. Mismatch estimated from sampled actions predicts these changes when the optimum is known, and for coding agents, teacher-based estimates of ceiling minus mismatch order harnesses by accuracy. Harness evaluations should therefore report the ceiling next to the frozen return, evaluate several checkpoints under each harness rather than single one, and check how presentation changes move the models choices. Harness distillation and joint adaptation of harnesses and weights (Ye et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026; Kim et al., 2026) can use sampled-action measurements to track the ceiling and the mismatch separately. Appendix discusses related work.

sections.title: A RELATED WORK
sections.content: Regularized control and decision geometry. Control as inference and RL with maximum entropy objective express optimal policies through rewards, action values, and reference distributions (Levine, 2018; Haarnoja et al., 2017; 2018). Regularized control supplies the Gibbs policy and the geometry of the value gap (Geist et al., 2019; ODonoghue, 2022). The relation between policy gradients and soft Q-learning provides another view of these coordinates (Schulman et al., 2017). DPO and its sequential extension relate language-model policies to rewards and action values during post-training (Rafailov et al., 2023; 2024). Our optimal action score combines the optimal semantic action value with the semantic reference prior. These coordinates let us compare the decisions induced by different interfaces and measure deployed policys gap to each optimum. The analysis of fine-tuning objectives by Swamy et al. (2025) likewise uses common geometric description to distinguish ideal equivalence from differences that emerge in practice. Here the distinction concerns the interfaces optimal decisions and the choices that particular checkpoint makes through it. Behavioral identification and reward transfer. Inverse RL recovers rewards from behavior subject to ambiguities (Ng & Russell, 2000; Russell, 1998). Reward shaping using potential function preserves optimal policies (Ng et al., 1999). Analyses of identifiability under entropy regularization and of partial identifiability characterize the corresponding reward classes (Cao et al., 2021; Skalse et al., 2023). EPIC compares reward functions while accounting for transformations that preserve policies (Gleave et al., 2021). Work on the transferability of rewards recovered through regularized inverse RL further studies changes in transition laws (Schlaginhaufen & Kamgarpour, 2024). Our equivalence class for single interface removes statewise constants from the scores. Appendix distinguishes this behavioral object from the nonunique decomposition into prior, reward, and transition. The transfer analysis then compares the target energy with the actual deployed readout, weighting their discrepancy by deployment occupancy. Interface and agent design. Interface design and prompt formatting affect agent behavior (Yang et al., 2024; Sclar et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025a). GUI-360 reports higher action prediction accuracy for GPT-4o and lower accuracy for fine-tuned Qwen after adding accessibility metadata and replacing coordinate arguments with element IDs (Mu et al., 2025). ADAS and AFlow search over agent implementations and workflows (Hu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025b). Darwin Gödel Machine and Self-Improving Coding Agent revise scaffolds and assess them through execution (Zhang et al., 2026; Robeyns et al., 2025). Promptbreeder, ToolMaker, and MAS-ZERO respectively explore prompts, tools, and designs involving multiple agents (Fernando et al., 2023; Wölflein et al., 2025; Ke et al., 2025). Surveys place these approaches within agent systems with mechanisms for self improvement (Fang et al., 2025; ang Gao et al., 2026). These design procedures can change action opportunities, realizations, or both. Our analysis separates each candidates optimal return from the evaluated checkpoints gap to that optimum. This distinction connects execution feedback to two possible sources of improvement: more useful decision problem and policy that better realizes its available decisions. Context and harness distillation. Context distillation trains model to reproduce, without the prompt, the behavior that the prompt elicits (Snell et al., 2022). Harness-Zero distills specialized harness into the weights by letting harnessing agent correct the students responses in the target harnesss action space (Ye et al., 2026). Our identification result states which decision information such training can carry, the relative action scores of the training harness. The readout study shows that the learned preferences are still expressed through the deployment interface, so distilled policy can change its choices when the interface changes. Joint adaptation of harnesses and model weights. Joint adaptation takes several forms: SIA selects harness and weight updates, Co-Harness trains from trajectories collected under revised interfaces, and WHALE alternates training with harness search (Hebbar et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026; Kim et al., 2026). Yu et al. (2026) find that imitating expert trajectories can hurt weaker model under an evolved harness while on-policy correction helps, and HarnessBandit schedules training across harnesses by learnability and transferability (Wei et al., 2026). 14 These methods can use the ceiling and the mismatch to tell whether candidate harness offers too little or is not yet used well. Our adaptation threshold specifies the mismatch reduction needed to make revision with higher ceiling beneficial. Eq. (24) isolates how weight update changes revisions relative value. Comparisons across checkpoints and interfaces therefore track both recovery after revision and changes in interface rankings. The controlled protocol measures this interaction separately from gains under either interface alone. This gives every checkpoint fixed optimal policy to compare against, while retaining task instructions, parameterized actions, and controller feedback in the models input. We compare six harnesses, H0H5, using H0 as the direct baseline. Tasks and observations. We use three tasks from MiniWoB++ (Liu et al., 2018). In click-checkboxes, the agent toggles checkboxes to match the requested labels and submits the selection.
